newsitem.title: GERMANY: Czech parliament chairman asks Bonn for pact rider.
newsitem.headline: Czech parliament chairman asks Bonn for pact rider.

text.p: Czech parliament chairman Milos Zeman asked Germany's parliamentary parties on Tuesday for a last-minute rider to a post-World War Two reconciliation accord, but German officials said he had little hope of success.

The declaration was signed by both countries' heads of government last week. It does not need formal ratification but the German parliament is due to vote on it on Thursday, and the Czech parliament early next month, to give it extra weight.

"(The Czech parliament's foreign affairs committee) asked me to negotiate about the possibility of a short introductory note," Zeman told reporters before a meeting with German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel. He said he had brought proposals for the German parliamentary parties.
Zeman's Social Democrats (CSSD), the largest Czech opposition party, have reservations about the text of the accord, hammered out during two years of tortuous negotiations.
In the accord, Bonn expresses sorrow for the 1938 to 1945 Nazi occupation of Czech land, and Prague its regret at Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of 2.5 million Germans.

But the declaration provides no compensation or redress for the expelled Germans whose property was confiscated, nor does it satisfy Czechs who wanted Germany to make a commitment that those people no longer entertained property claims.

The proposed preamble, to be attached in both parliaments to the motion to approve the declaration, would aim to allay the CSSD's concern that the pact does not affirm the legal validity of the expulsions and confiscations.
But German coalition party sources said they would not agree to any rider to the motion, which in its draft form says simply that the German parliament approves the declaration.

Karl Lamers, parliamentary foreign policy spokesman for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily it was out of the question that a rider could be added which would explicitly close the property issue.
The accord also remains controversial in Germany.
Most members of parliament for the Bavarian-based Christian Social Union, political mentors of the expelled Germans, say the declaration does not properly express the injustice done by the Czechs.
But they say they will vote for the declaration, despite its weaknesses, as a contribution to European integration.
